analysis.one_liner: Separates deposit-taking banks from investment banking, insurance, and swaps trading.
analysis.headline: The bill, which had 12 original sponsors including one Republican, was referred to two House committees, sent to a subcommittee, and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rebuild the wall between ordinary banking and Wall Street that stood from the 1930s until 1999. Banks that take insured deposits could no longer be affiliated with securities firms, insurance companies, or swaps dealers, could not trade for their own profit, underwrite securities, make markets, run hedge funds or private equity funds, or do prime brokerage. Existing combinations would have five years to unwind, and executives would have to certify compliance under penalty of perjury. The stated aim is to keep taxpayer-insured deposits out of risky trading and end conflicts of interest between banks and their customers.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary depositors and taxpayers, who would no longer have federally insured bank deposits backing securities trading, market making, and other high-risk activities at giant financial conglomerates. Community and regional banks that compete against too-big-to-fail institutions would also benefit from a more level playing field.

how_it_helps.text: Bars insured depository institutions from affiliating with, being under common control with, or acting as insurance companies, securities entities, or swaps entities, with existing affiliations terminated within five years.

Limits national banks to core banking services: taking deposits, extending credit, payment systems, coin and bullion, and customer-directed securities business, while prohibiting investment in structured or synthetic products.

Prohibits bank holding companies from proprietary trading, market-making, prime brokerage, and owning or sponsoring hedge funds or private equity funds, while allowing swaps only as an end-user hedge documented at inception.

Repeals the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act provisions that created financial holding companies, repeals national banks' authority to hold financial subsidiaries, and ends the special bankruptcy protections for derivatives and repurchase agreements that put those contracts ahead of other creditors.

Adds an anti-evasion rule with enforcement teeth: regulators can order termination of evasion activity, claw back a penalty of 10 percent of an entity's average net profits over three years, and pursue individuals involved, plus executive attestation under penalty of perjury.

analysis.who_pays: The largest universal banks and financial conglomerates, which would have to separate or divest their securities, insurance, swaps, hedge fund, and private equity operations within five years, and institutional clients of bank prime brokerage and market-making desks who would face a changed set of counterparties.

drawbacks.text: Forcing the breakup of existing bank conglomerates within five years, with extensions capped at one year, could be disruptive to financial markets and costly to execute, and companies receiving extensions must publicly disclose that they failed to comply.

Some analysts argue the 1999 repeal of Glass-Steagall was not the main cause of the 2008 crisis, and that the largest banks are already restricted by the Volcker Rule's proprietary-trading ban; the bill's own findings acknowledge the debate by citing both supportive and skeptical expert views, though its findings conclude separation reduces systemic risk.

Universal banks argue that combining commercial and investment banking lets them offer one-stop services and absorb shocks across business lines; this bill eliminates that model for U.S. banks even as it carves out traditional trust and fiduciary activities and end-user hedging.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is a reduced risk that taxpayers again backstop losses from securities trading done with insured deposits, and the removal of documented conflicts of interest between banks and their customers; the cost is borne almost entirely by the largest financial firms and their shareholders through forced separation, with some transition risk for markets. The bill is deliberately structured with a five-year phase-out, a narrow hedge exception, and public disclosure of noncompliance, which makes it a serious, rather than symbolic, restoration of the separation.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Financial Services and Judiciary committees and then to a Financial Services subcommittee, and neither committee ever scheduled it for consideration before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Michael Capuano introduced the bill on May 22, 2017 with seven original cosponsors, including Republican Rep. Walter Jones of North Carolina.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services and, in addition, to the House Committee on the Judiciary.

On June 23, 2017, the portion under Financial Services jurisdiction was referred to the Subcommittee on Regulatory Reform, Commercial and Antitrust Law; no further action of any kind appears in the record for the remainder of the Congress.
The bill ended with 11 cosponsors (10 Democrats, 1 Republican) and no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The largest universal banks and financial conglomerates are better off: nothing changed, so they kept the ability to run insured deposits, trading, underwriting, and swaps under one roof. Bank shareholders avoided a five-year forced breakup.

sides.party_line_note: Eleven of the twelve original sponsors were Democrats and the lone Republican was Rep. Walter Jones; the Republican-controlled Financial Services Committee took no action on the bill, so no votes were ever recorded.

industries.industry: Large universal banks and financial conglomerates
industries.note: These firms would have to unwind their combinations of insured deposits with securities, insurance, and swaps businesses within five years. They benefit from the current model because insured deposits and implicit too-big-to-fail support cheapen funding for risky trading, a cost that lands on taxpayers if things go wrong.

industries.industry: Securities underwriting, market-making, and prime brokerage
industries.note: Bank holding companies would be banned from underwriting, dealing, market-making, and prime brokerage, though banks could still buy and sell securities for customers' accounts and keep trust and fiduciary business. Independent securities firms would face less competition from deposit-funded bank affiliates.
Banks could no longer affiliate with registered swaps dealers and could buy swaps only as documented end-user hedges, shrinking the dealer franchise built on bank balance sheets.

Bank holding companies could no longer own, sponsor, or invest in these funds, cutting off a funding and distribution channel, while independent fund managers would face less bank-affiliated competition.

Insured depository institutions could not affiliate with or be commonly controlled with insurance companies, unwinding bank-insurer combinations, while standalone insurers would face less deposit-funded competition.

Smaller banks would benefit from a financial system where the largest rivals cannot cross-subsidize trading with insured deposits, though they also face the same core-banking limits on their own securities and structured-product activities.
